headline: New moon springs load up Plum Gut as fluke slide out of the warm bays
subhead: Bigger tides mean bigger current through the Gut and the Race — bass, blues, and porgies are all feeling it different ways.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound side did what it usually does the few days before a new moon — it got quiet on me. Current went soft, especially the middle of the week, and the fish that had been stacked on Horton Point rockpile scattered out looking for moving water. I don't chase fish when the tide's lazy like that, I go make coffee and wait. Wind sat out of the southwest most days, nothing heavy, but enough to keep the surface a little riled and the bait pushed tight to structure instead of spread out where you could find it easy. Water's been holding warm, the kind of warm that pushes bait and predators alike out of the shallow coves and into anything with current running through it — inlets, rips, the mouth of the Gut.

Now the moon's turning new right about today, and that means springs building through the weekend, peaking the 11th through 13th. Bigger tides, more water moving, harder current at Plum Gut and down through the Race. That's the kind of setup that wakes this whole stretch up. When the current's ripping through the Gut on the ebb, everything from bass to blues to the odd weakfish gets pushed into ambush position along the edges where the fast water meets the slow — and that's exactly where I want a bucktail or a diamond jig, not sitting in the middle of the pipe.

Fluke have been doing what fluke do this time of year when the back bays get too warm for their liking — they're sliding out. Anybody still working the flats behind Mattituck creek is finding smaller fish and fewer of them. The better ones have moved to the inlet itself, sitting on the edges of the channel where the outgoing tide dumps cooler water pulled off the Sound bottom. I've had decent results dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a three-quarter ounce bucktail right along that channel edge on the last two hours of the outgoing, working it slow, letting it bounce bottom. Nothing spectacular — a few keepers to 22 inches mixed with a lot of short fish — but it beats fishing empty water in the bay. If you're set up to fish the Sound side of the inlet mouth on that outgoing push, that's your play this week, and it should hold as long as the bay stays warm and keeps shoving fish out.

Bass have been a mixed bag, honestly, and I won't tell you different. Rocky Point and the rockpile off Horton have both given up fish, but you're working for them — covering water, hitting the tide change right, not just showing up and expecting the bite to find you. Best fish I heard of this week came off bunker chunks fished on the bottom during the last of the outgoing at Rocky Point, a fish pushing 30 pounds, but that was one report, not a pattern. Most guys are doing better with topwater and swimming plugs worked over the rockpiles at first light before the sun gets high, picking off schoolies and the occasional better fish holding tight to structure. With the springs building, I'd expect the bigger fish to start showing more consistently on the moving water — bass like current, and this weekend they're going to get plenty of it.

Bluefish have been around but not thick. Diamond jigs and small metal worked through the rip at the Plum Gut approach have connected, mostly on the last of the incoming when bait gets funneled through that pinch point. Nothing like the blitzes you sometimes get out there in August, but enough action to keep rods bent if you're willing to work the tide change and not just anchor up and wait.

Porgies and blackfish are the reliable part of the report right now, same as they always are this time of year. The structure off Rocky Point and around the Orient Point rockpiles is holding both. Porgies are eating clam and sandworm on high-low rigs in 15 to 25 feet, steady if unspectacular, good eating fish for anybody who wants a bucket to bring home. Blackfish are still a touch light for the season — you're picking through a lot of shorts to find keepers — but green crab fished tight to the rocks on the bottom stages of the tide has been productive enough that it's worth the trip if that's your game.

On the pelagic side, I keep hearing chatter about bonito working the eastern inlets on the clean incoming tide, and Plum Gut sits right in that corridor if the pattern holds. That window's supposed to close out soon, so if you've got a light spinning rod and some Deadly Dick jigs rigged up, this next week or so is the time to give it a shot on a clean incoming tide with good visibility. I haven't put my hands on one myself yet this year off my beat, but the conditions line up for it here as much as anywhere east of us.

Looking ahead — the new moon springs peaking Saturday through Monday are the story. Bigger tides, stronger current, better ambush points at the Gut and the Race. If I had one window to fish this week, I'd take the evening flood into sunset at the Plum Gut approach, working a bucktail or swimming plug through the seam where the fast water meets slack. That's where the bass and blues will be staging as the tide pushes hard behind them. Bring a backup rod rigged for porgy in case the current's too much to work metal clean — with springs this big, sometimes you need a Plan B while you figure out where the fish are sitting.
